books.section: Topic 6.12 Controversies over the Role of Government in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Joseph Keppler, “The Bosses of the Senate,” Puck, January 23, 1889

stimulus.text: The cartoon, “The Bosses of the Senate,” by Joseph Keppler in Puck magazine, January 23, 1889, shows the United States Senate chamber. Tiny senators sit at small desks in the lower half of the picture. Towering over them are huge men in top hats whose swollen bodies are money bags labeled with the names of trusts: “Standard Oil Trust,” “Copper Trust,” “Steel Beam Trust,” “Iron Trust,” “Sugar Trust,” “Coal Trust,” and “Nail Trust.” A sign on the wall reads: “This is a Senate of the Monopolists by the Monopolists and for the Monopolists!” A door at the left is marked “People’s Entrance” and “Closed.”
stimulus.source_note: Joseph Keppler, “The Bosses of the Senate,” Puck, January 23, 1889. Public domain; image viewed by the writer (new pool file: u6/u6-bosses-of-senate.jpg, catalogued in CATALOG-u6.json).

stem: Why would reformers in 1889 have welcomed this cartoon?

options.text: It proved that the Senate had already broken up the trusts by law
options.misconception: The cartoon shows the trusts in command, not broken up.

options.text: It made the hidden influence of trusts visible and built support for regulation
It showed that senators had no ties to business at all
options.misconception: The cartoon shows senators dwarfed by business, the opposite of no ties.

options.text: It argued that monopolies should elect senators directly to protect their interests
options.misconception: The cartoon attacks trust control; it does not ask trusts to elect senators.

rationales.A: The trusts tower over the chamber, so nothing here shows them broken up.
rationales.B: A picture of money bags ruling the Senate lets readers see the influence reformers attacked.
rationales.C: The senators sit beneath the trusts, which is a picture of ties to business.
rationales.D: Keppler mocks trust control of the Senate; he never asks for more of it.
rationales.general:
Ask what the picture could do for reformers.
1. The cartoon turns an unseen influence into figures anyone can see.
2. Labeled trusts loom over tiny senators under a mocking sign.
3. Readers who see the picture can feel the Senate belongs to monopolists.
4. Background from the books: that public feeling helped carry the Sherman Antitrust Act in 1890.
Remember: a cartoon reforms by making the hidden visible.
